title: Is it good idea to tell other people about your game ideas?
author: Practical-Aide-2550
selftext: I'm at the early stage of making my first game. I'm about 10 % done on my game. I'm scared people my steal my idea and make the game before me and make me look like I copy them.

replies.author: RedTheRobot
replies.body:
Anyone can make anything ideas are actually the weak point. There are 7 billion people on earth the odds of having an idea truly unique are slim. Specially if that idea is based on existing platforms such as a PC game. 

You even described your game as similar to plague inc. If you can describe it as similar to something else then again it isn’t that unique. 

Look at it another way say I wanted to create a new soda (game) and I said it is like coke but with a twist like I add in apple flavor. Should I be worried coke will steal my idea? No because the idea isn’t important the community you create around your product is. Big companies can’t compete in the community space. Customers will never be able to tell the CEO of coke they should replace apple with orange but a small company can listen and make changes to the original idea.

Honestly, It might be good to get feedback from other on your ideas.   
Game design is pretty complex. 

Unless you have something truly unique no one is going to steal it. 

Even if they took your basic and made another game based on it, it wouldn't be anything like yours. 

Look at how many 1st person shooters, rouge likes, top down shooters, bullet hells, Turn based card battlers, gotcha games, etc. 

It's not like your there is room for many many different games in the same genre.

comments.author: syn_krown
comments.body:
Then dont tell anyone. The reason you want to tell someone is for the dopamine, you wee addict.

When you tell someone your idea, not only does it give them a chance to steal it, but you get the satisfaction that you would have received when finishing the idea, which can make you less enthusiastic naturally. 

Wait until you have something solid to produce, then tell people. And dont tell people on an AI forum, cause if your inexperienced ass can make it, there's gonna be those who could make it properly

comments.author: A_Sword_Saint
comments.body:
When you go to actually build your idea you will encounter 1000 problems. In order to keep moving forward you will need to solve those problems and inevitably this will change how your idea actually works in reality. After solving those you will eventually show your game to playtesters and realize there are 1000 more problems to fix that will change your idea. This will keep happening until you hopefully actually finish. 

By the time you are done, your actual game will have drifted in many ways from the original idea. It will have been battletested and refined in so many ways you couldn't even explain them all if asked. Someone who heard your initial idea would have done the same and by the time they finished thier idea would have also drifted from the original idea but in different ways than you chose.

At best your initial idea would just be a starting point even if someone decided to "copy" you.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
If the game is simple enough for them to take a quick idea and run with it into success before you, then maybe keep it to yourself if you're not pushing it out immediately. For instance, if you had the idea for some brand new viral game like Flappy Bird/Angry Birds/?, that is a simple enough idea and game that another person could program it within a week and have it selling in no time. That being said... if your idea is that simple, there is no reason for you to not already have it out there before telling anyone about it.

If the game is far more complex, it really doesn't matter if someone gleans some insight from it, because whatever they produce would be dramatically different. You could tell someone, "I want to make an RPG where you play as a goblin that can grow and evolve into other monster species as you get more powerful!" and even if someone went and tried doing the same thing, I imagine the execution would be so different it wouldn't matter. I think it's most concerning when it comes to specifically unique mechanics that might be easy to implement but would define your game.  An example would be Moonsigil Atlas's mana-replacement mechanic (the hexagon tile placement) or Balatro using traditional poker hands for its  scoring mechanisms. Like... maybe keep those kinds of things to yourself until your game is far along in development because they are fairly easy to harness as ideas and whether you're the first to do it might make or break your game.

If you're just building on established formulas, there isn't much to hide. But if you think you're reinventing a genre or have something totally new, keep it to people you are close to that you trust. But you'll have to find a balance between getting opinions and testing vs keeping your cards close to your chest. Most game devs, though, have specific games they already want to make, and won't give two shits about your game and its idea even if it's great, because it's not the game they want to make/play. There are some dumbasses who go into game dev thinking it's a good way to make money though (it's not, relative to the time investment at least) who are just looking to make a quick buck and have no ideas of their own, and those might be predatory enough that they'd at least try to create some version of it.
